project.name: local-ai-packaged
project.description: Self-hosted, Docker Compose template that bootstraps a full local AI and low-code development environment — Ollama for local LLMs, n8n for low-code automation, Open WebUI, Flowise, Supabase, Qdrant, Neo4j, Langfuse, SearXNG, and Caddy. This checkout extends the base template with an n8n multi-agent pipeline, a cc-observability platform (TS/Vue + OpenTelemetry), a Backstage developer portal, and Python orchestration scripts. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what this project is: an open Docker Compose template that bootstraps a full Local AI + Low-Code development environment (Ollama, Open WebUI, Supabase, Flowise, Qdrant, Neo4j, SearXNG, Langfuse, Caddy) running under a single 'localai' Compose project. The README also outlines how this checkout extends the base template with five major sub-systems: an n8n multi-agent PRD/architecture pipeline, a cc-observability platform, a Backstage developer portal, OpenCode/Claude ArchiMate tooling, and healthcare knowledge bases. Read this first to get the map for the rest of the tour.

tour.title: The Startup Orchestrator
tour.description: start_services.py is the project's true entry point. It clones the Supabase 'docker/' subtree, copies the root .env into Supabase, generates the SearXNG secret, handles first-run permissions, then launches the Supabase stack followed by the local-AI stack so both share one Docker network and project name. This single script is what turns a checkout into a running environment, and understanding its sequence explains why two separate Compose files behave as one stack.
tour.languageLesson: This Python orchestrator shells out to 'docker compose' with --profile flags (cpu, gpu-nvidia, gpu-amd, none). Compose profiles let one file describe multiple deployment shapes, and the script selects which services start based on the chosen GPU profile.

tour.title: The Compose Stack & Secrets
tour.description: docker-compose.yml is the heart of the runtime: it defines n8n, Ollama (with CPU/GPU profiles), Open WebUI, Flowise, Qdrant, Neo4j, Caddy and the supporting services, all wired onto the shared network from Step 2. The .env.example file enumerates every secret and hostname the stack needs (encryption keys, Postgres password, Supabase JWT keys, Neo4j auth, Langfuse credentials). Together they show how services discover each other via internal Docker hostnames and where configuration is injected.
tour.languageLesson: Compose services reference each other by service name as DNS hostnames on the shared network (e.g. http://ollama:11434, http://qdrant:6333). Compose profiles attached to the Ollama service let the same file run CPU-only or GPU-accelerated without edits.

tour.title: Reverse Proxy & Chat Bridge
tour.description: Caddy is the single front door for the whole stack. The Caddyfile routes each service to a localhost port in development and to a custom HTTPS domain in production via Let's Encrypt. n8n_pipe.py closes the loop on the user experience: it is an Open WebUI 'pipe' function that forwards chat messages to an n8n webhook, letting the chat interface invoke the pre-built RAG agent workflows the README advertises. These two files explain how external traffic reaches services and how the chat UI talks to automation.

tour.title: n8n Multi-Agent Pipeline
tour.description: The first major extension is an n8n agent pipeline that turns a request into a PRD and then a full architecture. The start-here README and the master orchestrator workflow describe a fan-out pattern where one orchestrator coordinates specialist sub-workflows. The refactored ack workflow shows the production shape: a set of webhook receivers (business analysis, architecture, project management, quality/compliance) that hand work between agents. This is the low-code automation layer the platform is built to run.

tour.title: Pipeline Database Schema
tour.description: The n8n pipeline persists its state in Postgres (provided by the Supabase stack from Step 2). The end-to-end schema defines e2e_projects as the root entity, with functional_requirements, shared_context, expert_consultations, and prd_documents hanging off each project. The migration-tracking schema adds migrations, approval_gates, artifacts, and execution_logs so the orchestrator can resume runs and gate progress. Reading these schemas reveals the data model that the workflows in Step 5 read and write.
tour.languageLesson: These SQL files declare foreign-key relationships (e.g. requirements and documents referencing a project id) so the pipeline's data stays normalized. Migration scripts should be ordered and idempotent so the same schema can be reapplied as the pipeline evolves.

tour.title: Pipeline Architecture Guide
tour.description: Building on the workflows and schema from Steps 5-6, this guide documents the full architecture pipeline end to end: how a request flows through the agents, where artifacts are stored, and how to run it. Use it as the narrative companion to the workflow JSON, which is otherwise hard to read directly. It connects the human-facing pipeline concepts to the concrete tables and webhooks you just examined.

tour.title: Multi-Agent ArchiMate Tooling
tour.description: The OpenCode/Claude agent tooling is the largest sub-system in the repo. Specialist agents are defined as markdown prompts: the architect-orchestrator coordinates the run, the BA agent emits a structured BRD in JSON mode, and the app-architect translates business architecture into application architecture. This agent-definition-as-document pattern lets the same prompts drive ArchiMate/C4 model generation across providers, and it mirrors the role split you saw in the n8n pipeline.

tour.title: Architecture JSON Transformers
tour.description: The agents in Step 8 produce architecture as structured JSON; these Python scripts turn that JSON into deliverables. json-to-archimate.py emits ArchiMate Exchange XML (the project's default model format), json-to-markdown.py renders human-readable BRD/PRD docs, and json-to-sql.py generates DDL. They are the deterministic 'last mile' that converts agent output into the files architects and developers actually consume.
tour.languageLesson: ArchiMate Exchange Format is an OpenGroup XML schema (http://www.opengroup.org/xsd/archimate/3.0/) consumable by both Archi and ADOIT. These transformers assign stable element identifiers so the generated XML round-trips cleanly into modeling tools.

tour.title: Knowledge & RAG Seeding
tour.description: GraphRAG and vector search need a populated knowledge base. setup-qdrant-collections.py creates the Qdrant vector collections (matching the embedding dimensions), and embed-documents.py chunks source documents, generates embeddings, and upserts them into the store. These scripts seed the Qdrant/Neo4j vector and graph stores that the README highlights, turning the raw infrastructure from Step 3 into a queryable knowledge layer the agents can draw on.

tour.title: Healthcare Knowledge Bases
tour.description: The repo ships domain knowledge for the IFHAS/Sahatna healthcare architecture work. The Sahatna technology-stack document catalogs the existing landscape (cloud platform, data, integration) and is one of the most-referenced documents in the graph, while the reference-architectures index organizes target patterns. This is the curated source material that the embedding pipeline in Step 10 ingests and the agents in Step 8 consult when generating healthcare architectures.

tour.title: Observability Platform
tour.description: cc-observability is a self-contained TypeScript/Vue app that tracks Claude Code activity via OpenTelemetry spans. server/index.ts wires up the HTTP/WebSocket server, routing, CORS and OTel; types.ts is the shared event/span/session vocabulary that the highest fan-in code in this sub-system depends on; and App.vue hosts the dashboard UI. It captures the agent runs from Steps 8-9 so their behavior becomes observable.
tour.languageLesson: OpenTelemetry models work as spans (timed operations) grouped into traces. The server exports spans to SQLite and streams live updates to the Vue client over a WebSocket, so the dashboard reflects activity in near real time.

tour.title: Observability Hooks & Container
tour.description: The platform receives data through Claude Code hooks. lib.ts is the shared helper (highest fan-in in the sub-system) that reads stdin and resolves context, and send-event.ts POSTs the resulting event payloads to the server from Step 12. The Dockerfile then packages the whole app: a multi-stage Bun build that compiles the client and installs server dependencies separately before copying only runtime artifacts into a slim final image.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use several FROM stages: build stages hold dev dependencies and compile output, while the final slim stage copies only what the app needs at runtime, keeping the image small.

tour.title: Backstage Developer Portal
tour.description: Backstage is the internal developer portal (the ADHDS Marketplace) that catalogs the stack's services. index.tsx mounts the app, App.tsx wires plugins and routes, and app-config.yaml configures the catalog and integrations. Backstage catalog descriptors register stack services like Caddy and SearXNG as components, giving teams a single place to discover and navigate everything assembled in the earlier steps.

tour.title: Backstage Containerization
tour.description: As a capstone, the Backstage Dockerfile shows how the portal is built and shipped: a multi-stage build whose first stage installs dependencies with Yarn and compiles the app, and whose final stage runs on a slim node:22 image with only the production bundle. This mirrors the containerization pattern from Step 13 and completes the picture of how every sub-system in this monorepo gets packaged for deployment alongside the core localai stack.
tour.languageLesson: Layer ordering matters for Docker cache efficiency: dependency installation is placed before copying application source so that code-only changes do not invalidate the (slower) dependency layer on rebuilds.
